I'm sorry but equating poor internet access with genocides, slavery and gulags or homelessness and starvation is just stupid and wrong. The person who should be mocked isn't the one who had the gall to NOT go along with such a false equivalence. It's the one who asserted it in the first place.
You're the only one equating poor internet access with those things. I didn't say it was a human right to have internet but in the modern age it is kind of a necessity.

Sorry, I was speaking to the mindset in the article more than what you actually said. The article implies that what O'Rielly said was outrageous when it's not.

Calling something a human right, or a human necessity in the context of a public policy dispute like this is a cheap rhetorical trick that trivializes the concept of human rights. O'Rielly's opponents on the policy issue are not saying that universal internet access is a good idea or necessary policy which would be fine arguments. They're saying instead that failure to supply internet access is a human rights violation putting it in the same league as shuffling political prisoners off to concentration camps. Or that it is a human necessity equivalent to letting people starve or freeze in the streets.

There are disputes which merit such language. Even now we face issues of war and torture which really, really do merit such language. Debates about utility subsidies, or the fine points of utility regulation really just don't merit that kind of language. It's insulting to speak of that kind of thing in those terms. Sorry again, that kind of hyperbolic moral posturing over relatively minor disputes is a pet peeve.
